title: Runs that outlive the request
brief: A task will run for hours and may wait a day for a human. Run length, tool failure rate, approval delay and whether side effects can safely repeat are all open. Decide where state lives and how a run resumes.

blocks.text: State outside the process, side effects outside the replay

blocks.title: Where a long run lives
blocks.intro: Anthropic's lesson from production: agents are stateful and errors compound, so resume from where the run was instead of restarting, with retry logic and regular checkpoints [[r2]].

options.name: In-process loop
options.summary: The loop runs in one process and keeps state in memory.
cons: A crash or deploy loses the run
A human wait ties up a worker
options.bestWhen: Runs last minutes, restarting is cheap and no paid side effects occur.
options.avoidWhen: Runs last hours, wait for people or trigger paid actions.

options.name: Framework checkpoints
options.summary: Write state at defined points and resume from the last one. Agent Framework writes a checkpoint at the end of each superstep, capturing executor state, pending messages, pending requests and responses, and shared state [[r21]]. LangGraph checkpointers store thread-scoped state [[r43]], and interrupt() needs a checkpointer and a thread_id [[r44]].
cons: Side effects can still repeat on resume
An in-memory saver loses state on restart
options.bestWhen: Runs take minutes to hours and you already run the framework.
options.avoidWhen: You need deterministic replay or very long timers.

options.name: Durable orchestration
options.summary: Orchestration code is replayed from a history. Temporal runs code as Durable Execution, with deterministic workflow code and side effects in Activities that carry retry policies, timeouts and heartbeats [[r42]]. Agent Framework's Durable Extension targets Azure Functions or your own compute [[r12]].
pros: Waits cost no compute and no model tokens while idle [[r12]]
cons: More platform to learn and operate
The Durable Extension page states no GA status and installs with a prerelease flag (--prerelease for .NET, --pre for pip) as of 2026-10-13
options.bestWhen: Runs last hours to days, wait on approvals or trigger paid or irreversible effects.
options.avoidWhen: Runs are short and a restart is cheap.

options.name: Managed asynchronous run
options.summary: A platform holds the run. OpenAI background mode lets you poll the response until it leaves queued and in_progress, and cancel it [[r25]]. Anthropic's Managed Agents (beta, header managed-agents-2026-04-01) separates session, harness and sandbox, and a new harness resumes with wake(sessionId) [[r15]].
pros: State and sandbox are managed for you
cons: Retention rules apply: without an explicit store=true a background response is deleted after roughly 10 minutes [[r25]]
Less control over replay and versions
options.bestWhen: You want long runs without owning the runtime and can accept the vendor's retention and beta status.
options.avoidWhen: Data residency, retention or isolation rules need your own control.

meta.v: background mode has no beta label on its page, Managed Agents beta, as of 2026-10-13

blocks.title: Life of a long-running run
blocks.alt: State diagram: a run moves between running, waiting for a human and failed, and ends as done or stopped.
blocks.src:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Running
  Running --> Waiting: approval needed
  Waiting --> Running: human responds
  Running --> Failed: crash or tool error
  Failed --> Running: resume from checkpoint
  Running --> Stopped: budget hit
  Running --> Done: goal met
  Done --> [*]
  Stopped --> [*]
blocks.caption: Every transition writes state. Waiting costs nothing when the platform parks the run durably.
What makes a resume safe depends on the kind of step.
head: Step type
Safe to repeat?
What makes resume safe
Example
rows: Retry with backoff and a cap
Client-generated idempotency key reused on retry [[r26]]
Persist the key and outcome before moving on, and check state before re-issuing
Charge a card, send an email
A compensating step registered for each completed step [[r27]]
A durable wait with a timeout and an escalation path

items.symptom: After a crash the customer is charged twice
items.cause: Resume re-ran the step with a new idempotency key
items.fix: Generate the key once per logical operation, persist it with the checkpoint and reuse it. Stripe allows up to 255 characters and may prune v1 keys after 24 hours, so after a long wait check the outcome before re-issuing [[r26]].

items.symptom: A resumed run behaves differently from the original
items.cause: Replay is non-deterministic: orchestration code reads the clock, random numbers or live data
items.fix: Keep orchestration deterministic, move side effects into retried activities and replay stored results [[r42]].

items.symptom: The agent tries to finish everything in one pass, or declares success early
items.cause: Harness failure modes Anthropic saw: one-shotting the job and declaring done too early. Compaction alone was not enough.
items.fix: An initializer that writes a progress file and a first git commit, one increment per session, a clean state at the end and tests before marking done [[r14]].

items.symptom: Runs vanish or restart from zero after a deploy
items.cause: State lives in memory, or versions are replaced in place while runs sit mid-process
items.fix: Durable checkpoint store and rainbow deployments, where old and new versions run together while traffic shifts [[r2]].

items.symptom: A model change breaks a harness workaround
items.cause: Anthropic saw context anxiety on Sonnet 4.5 that disappeared on Opus 4.5, so harness assumptions go stale [[r15]]
items.fix: Re-test workarounds on every model change and delete the ones that no longer help.

blocks.title: A checkpoint is not durable execution
blocks.md: A checkpoint lets a run resume. It does not make a side effect safe to repeat, and it does not make replay deterministic. In Agent Framework for Python, from 1.13.0 an entry checkpoint is also written before the first superstep and when responses to request events arrive, with minor breaking changes [[r21]]. Pair checkpoints with idempotency keys and compensating steps, and put approvals behind a durable wait so nothing idles on a held worker.

quiz.q: A payment tool call times out sometimes. What is the bug in this retry loop?
options: Three attempts are too few for a payment call that may time out repeatedly under heavy load
A uuid4 value is never accepted as an idempotency key by a payment API
A charge call must never be retried once any timeout has been observed
The key is created inside the loop, so a retry after a timeout can charge a second time
quiz.explain: An idempotency key only protects a retry if the same key is reused. A fresh key per attempt tells the server each attempt is a new operation. The attempt count is not the defect, random UUIDs are a normal key format, and retrying is fine when the key is stable.

quiz.q: Put the steps of a safe resume after a crash in order.
items: Load the latest checkpoint for the run
Check whether the pending step's effect already happened
Re-issue the effect with its stored idempotency key if it did not
Continue the loop and write the next checkpoint
quiz.explain: State comes first, then a check against the source of truth, then a repeat that is safe because the key is stored. Writing the next checkpoint last records that the step is complete. Re-issuing before checking risks a duplicate once a key has been pruned.

quiz.q: An approval step can take up to 24 hours. Which design wastes the least while it waits?
options: A durable wait that parks the run and uses no compute or model tokens while idle
A polling loop in the agent process that calls the model every minute to ask whether the human has answered
An HTTP request held open with a 24-hour timeout on a long-lived worker
Restarting the whole run from the beginning when the human finally replies
quiz.explain: Durable orchestration parks the run and costs nothing while idle, and Microsoft says a 24-hour approval costs only seconds of execution on Flex Consumption. Polling burns tokens, a held request ties up a worker and breaks on any deploy, and restarting repeats work and side effects.

takeaways: Resume, do not restart: state belongs in a durable store, not in process memory.
A checkpoint helps you resume, but side effects still need idempotency keys or compensating steps.
Park human approvals behind a durable wait so idle time costs no compute or tokens.
Check status before promising production use: the Durable Extension states no GA status and Managed Agents is in beta as of 2026-10-13.
